qs.q: A patient receiving treatment for a systemic fungal infection is given flucytosine in combination with amphotericin B. Inside the fungal cell, what is the ultimate biochemical conversion that produces the active antimetabolite?
o: Conversion to 5‑fluorouracil by fungal cytosine deaminase
Phosphorylation by fungal thymidine kinase to the active triphosphate
Methylation by fungal transmethylases producing active purine analogs
Deamination by fungal adenosine deaminase yielding active uracil
Acetylation by fungal acetyltransferases that inhibit cell‑wall synthesis
qs.e: Fungal cytosine deaminase converts flucytosine intracellularly into 5-fluorouracil, which disrupts RNA and DNA synthesis.
qs.s: Weekly Pharmacology Exam - October 30, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: A patient being treated with Amphotericin B for a severe systemic fungal infection develops acute rises in serum creatinine. Which intervention is most appropriate to mitigate this major adverse effect?
o: Administering pre-hydration before intravenous infusion
Switching immediately to an alternative echinocandin
Adding a high-ceiling loop diuretic to the regimen
Co-administering topical clotrimazole for protection
qs.e: Nephrotoxicity is a major side effect of amphotericin B, and pre-hydration helps protect renal function. Switching to an echinocandin is unnecessary if treating systemic fungi like Cryptococcus where amphotericin B is preferred.

qs.q: A patient presents with a systemic fungal infection. Culture at 37°C yields a yeast form, while culture at 25°C yields a mould form. Which organism fits this description?
o: Candida albicans
Cryptococcus neoformans
Histoplasma capsulatum
Aspergillus fumigatus
qs.e: Histoplasma capsulatum is a dimorphic fungus that exists as a yeast at 37°C and a mould at 25°C. Cryptococcus and Aspergillus do not share this exact temperature-dependent dimorphic dual morphology in the same manner.
qs.s: Medical Fungi: Classification, Morphology, Reproduction & Spores: MCQs

qs.q: Amphotericin B, a polyene antifungal, would typically be used to treat all of the following severe systemic fungal infections EXCEPT:
o: Cryptococcal meningitis infection
Systemic candidiasis infection
Onychomycosis (tinea unguium)
Disseminated histoplasmosis disease
qs.e: Amphotericin B is a potent broad-spectrum antifungal reserved for severe, life-threatening systemic infections. Tinea unguium (onychomycosis) is a superficial/cutaneous infection typically treated with oral azoles or terbinafine, not amphotericin B due to its toxicity profile.

ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: Systemic fungal infections are invasive diseases caused by fungi that spread beyond the skin or mucosa, often affecting immunocompromised hosts. Prompt recognition, appropriate laboratory testing, and early antifungal therapy are essential to reduce mortality.

sections.p: Fungi that cause systemic disease enter the bloodstream or deep tissues, leading to organ dysfunction. Common agents include Candida, Cryptococcus, Histoplasma, Coccidioides, and Aspergillus.
b: Most occur in patients with weakened immunity (HIV, chemotherapy, transplant).
Geography matters: Histoplasma in Ohio River Valley, Coccidioides in Southwest US, etc.

sections.p: These fungi are eukaryotic, have cell walls containing β‑glucan and chitin, and many produce a polysaccharide capsule (e.g., Cryptococcus) that evades host defenses.
b: Dimorphic species change form in tissue (yeast) vs environment (mold).

sections.p: Entry routes include inhalation of spores, translocation from mucosal surfaces, or direct inoculation via catheters. Some dimorphic fungi convert to yeast after inhalation, disseminating hematogenously.
b: Candida often originates from gut or skin colonisation.

sections.p: Clinical syndromes range from candidemia to cryptococcal meningitis, disseminated histoplasmosis, coccidioidal pneumonia, and invasive aspergillosis. Severity is staged by organ involvement and host immune status.
b: Candidemia: fever, sepsis, possible end‑organ emboli.
Cryptococcal meningitis: headache, neck stiffness, raised ICP.
Invasive aspergillosis: sinusitis, pulmonary nodules, hemoptysis.

sections.p: Combine clinical suspicion with targeted laboratory tests. Culture, antigen detection, and molecular assays are key; imaging supports organ involvement.
b: Cryptococcal antigen in serum/CSF is highly sensitive.

t.b: Is a viable fungus present in the bloodstream? Positive growth confirms candidemia; negative does not rule out infection if prior antifungals.
Is Cryptococcus circulating? Positive indicates disseminated disease; titers guide severity.
Is Aspergillus invading? Positive supports invasive aspergillosis; false positives occur with certain antibiotics.
Is disseminated histoplasmosis present? Positive in most severe cases; cross‑reactivity with Blastomyces.
What is the pattern of organ involvement? Nodules with halo sign suggest aspergillosis; miliary pattern suggests histoplasmosis.

sections.p: First‑line therapy uses agents that penetrate the infected site and have fungicidal activity. Amphotericin B (deoxycholate or lipid formulations) and azoles are mainstays; echinocandins are preferred for candidemia.
b: Amphotericin B: broad spectrum, CNS penetration, but nephrotoxic.
Fluconazole: good for Candida and Cryptococcus, oral step‑down.
Voriconazole: drug of choice for invasive aspergillosis, excellent lung/brain levels.
Echinocandins (caspofungin, micafungin): safe for candidemia, no renal toxicity.

sections.p: Focus on host risk factors, typical organ involvement, key diagnostic tests, and first‑line antifungal choices.
b: Remember cryptococcal antigen is the fastest way to diagnose meningitis.
In neutropenic patients with fever unresponsive to antibiotics, think invasive aspergillosis.
Echinocandins are preferred for candidemia when renal function is poor.

whenToSeekHelp: New neurological deficits or signs of meningitis
Severe respiratory distress with hemoptysis in immunocompromised patients

faq.q: Why are fungal infections more common in HIV patients?
faq.a: HIV depletes CD4+ T cells, impairing the immune response needed to control intracellular fungi like Cryptococcus.

faq.q: Can a negative culture rule out systemic fungal infection?
faq.a: No; prior antifungal therapy or low organism burden can give false‑negative cultures, so antigen or molecular tests are essential.

faq.q: When is amphotericin B preferred over azoles?
faq.a: In severe, life‑threatening disease (e.g., cryptococcal meningitis, disseminated histoplasmosis) where rapid fungicidal activity and CNS penetration are needed.
